strengths: Addresses an important question: which latent information multimodal contrastive learning recovers. Modeling modalities through distinct, noisily coupled latent variables is a useful conceptual formulation.
Synthetic experiments cover matched assumptions and several distributional mismatches, reporting high recovery scores using both linear regression and component matching.

FastICA provides simple post-processing of pretrained representations. Reported experiments span four CLIP encoders and several distribution shifts; for example, two-shot ViT-B/16 target-average accuracy improves from 32.51 to 37.13.
weaknesses: The central proofs contain a fundamental contradiction. Appendices A.4.1 and A.5.1 require identical representations for every positive pair (Eqs. 27 and 49). The stipulated finite-noise conditional distributions have full support, so this condition forces constant representations, contradicting the simultaneous uniformity and latent-recovery requirements. Minimizing the combined contrastive objective does not require separately minimizing its alignment term. Consequently, the main identifiability claims lack valid proofs.

The cross-entropy reductions have additional substantive gaps. Appendix A.3 treats fixed-bandwidth kernel smoothing as the underlying density without establishing the required limit. For convex bodies, Lemma 4.2 establishes uniformity only as lambda approaches zero, but Eq. 56 uses exact uniformity at finite lambda. Truncation at the boundary generally makes the second modality's marginal nonuniform. Theorem 3.2 therefore does not follow under its stated assumptions.

The theoretical justification for ICA is missing even if linear identifiability is granted. A uniform hyperspherical distribution is rotationally invariant, so every orthogonal basis has the same population non-Gaussianity statistics; ICA cannot identify preferred latent axes from that distribution. Applying PCA to CLIP features also does not establish the convex-body assumptions or permutation-identifiability guarantee.

The downstream evaluation cannot attribute improvements to disentanglement. With standard whitening, FastICA contributes an orthogonal rotation of whitened features, under which the stated L2-regularized logistic regression objective is invariant. Dimensionality-matched PCA and whitening baselines are essential. The pipelines also use different component counts: 300 for ICA versus 160 or 200 for PCA plus ICA.

The CelebA evidence is qualitative and selectively presented. Counting 16 visually interpreted traversal attributes and comparing this with counts reported in separate FactorVAE and beta-TCVAE papers is not a controlled comparison. Quantitative disentanglement measurements, changes to unintended attributes, and matched reconstruction baselines are absent. These traversals do not validate latent identifiability.

Reproducibility and reporting are insufficient: synthetic sample sizes, encoder training settings, and repeat counts are missing; real-data results lack uncertainty estimates; and the PCA/ICA fitting data are unclear. Appendix A.8's reference to validation splits of each dataset leaves target-domain model selection ambiguous. Table 3 also misreports the RN101 baseline target average as 20.03; its listed entries average to 22.03.
